title: Renormalization Group Domain Walls from Phantom Symmetries
abstract: We develop a systematic construction of renormalization group (RG) domain walls between two-dimensional rational conformal field theories. Using phantom currents, we consider an auxiliary chiral extension linked to the folded ultraviolet--infrared theory by a topological interface. The construction of RG walls then reduces to identifying suitable automorphism-twisted Cardy states in the auxiliary theory. We find two such types of automorphisms: outer automorphisms exchanging identical current algebra factors, as in Gaiotto's construction, and continuous inner automorphisms generated by the zero modes of spin-one phantom currents. In the latter case, the RG domain walls generically admit a continuous defect conformal manifold. We further show that, when an RG flow can be orbifolded to another one, the orbifold may lift defect conformal moduli of the RG brane constructed using inner automorphisms. The two types of RG branes can then be mapped to each other via a topological interface defined by the orbifold. We demonstrate the two types of RG brane construction via various examples of flows between non-unitary minimal models, from parafermions to minimal models, and between generalized parafermions. Many physical observables of the RG walls are computed non-perturbatively, including boundary entropies and spectra, and UV--IR operator mixings. We also find interesting nontrivial boundary monodromy: a closed cycle in the defect conformal moduli space can carry an RG domain wall into other distinct non-trivial conformal interfaces.
summary: This paper provides a systematic algebraic construction for understanding Renormalization Group domain walls connecting different 2D Conformal Field Theories. By utilizing phantom symmetries and automorphism groups, the authors classify two types of RG interfaces and calculate key non-perturbative physical observables. This work offers a powerful mathematical tool for analyzing quantum phase transitions in strongly correlated matter.
main_problem: The paper develops a systematic method to construct Renormalization Group (RG) domain walls connecting two-dimensional rational conformal field theories (RCFTs). This addresses how physical theories flow between different fixed points.
main_result: The construction yields two types of RG walls—those from outer automorphisms and continuous families from inner automorphisms—and demonstrates how these can be mapped onto each other via an orbifold interface.
method: The method uses an auxiliary chiral extension and relies on identifying suitable automorphism-twisted Cardy states within this auxiliary theory.
model_or_system: The study focuses on RG flows between various CFTs, including non-unitary minimal models, parafermion theories, and generalized parafermion models.
key_observables: Boundary entropies, spectra, UV–IR operator mixings, and boundary monodromy.
important_parameters: The structure depends on the existence of preserved Topological Defect Lines (TDLs) and the specific automorphisms (outer vs. inner).
main_assumptions: The initial construction assumes the UV and IR theories are RCFTs, and the analysis relies on the algebraic structure provided by the auxiliary theory.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the half-space construction of an RG domain wall using a relevant operator perturbation, while Figure 2 shows the folding and shrinking of a transmitted TDL onto the RG brane.
paper_structure: The paper builds by first establishing the general algebraic framework using auxiliary theories and automorphisms, then detailing the two types of RG walls (outer vs. inner), demonstrating these constructions with specific examples (minimal models, parafermions), and finally calculating non-perturbative observables.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical framework connecting RG flow structures to algebraic symmetries (automorphisms) is highly relevant for understanding quantum critical points and boundary physics in strongly correlated systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Half-space construction of an RG domain wall. A perturbation given by a relevant operator is switched on for x < 0. The dashed magenta line denotes the interface during the flow, which need not be conformal. The solid magenta line denotes the RG wall after both the perturbed bulk and the interface interactions have reached their fixed points.

Figure 2. Folding and shrinking a transmitted TDL. Black dots denote chiral IR and anti-chiral UV endpoint fields before folding, and their combined chiral field O(h) s afterwards. The dashed line is the transmitted TDL, which becomes bLs in the folded theory TA. Shrinking its segment brings the endpoint field to the RG brane (magenta) as a boundary operator of the same dimension h.

Figure 3. Transport between RG branes for orbifold related RG flows. The green dashed line is the topological interface IG between the original and orbifold UV theories, with the common IR factor unchanged. Fusing it into the outer RG brane (magenta) removes the intervening orbifold strip and produces the inner RG brane at the distinguished moduli point ⃗φ∗.

Figure 4. Self-annulus spectrum of R211(φ) between the RG angle φ∗= π and the factorized point φ = 0. Blue and red curves show primary weights extracted from the two remainders Fφ and Jφ defined in Appendix A. Dashed lines are the known constant levels. The additional dotted primary and the descendant shown in purple approach h = 1 from above. Black points give the independently known factorized spectrum, with multiplicities indicated when larger than one.

Figure 5. A TIM spin-mixing channel through the composed Potts–M5,6–TIM interface. The green dashed and magenta lines denote Itop and IRG. The arrows follow a nonzero mixing channel from σT to Φ2,2, not an operator identity across the RG wall. Gauging turns this v-odd field into the Potts defect field µc, with h = ¯h = 1/40, attached to the charge conjugation line. The line ends on Itop. The Φ2,4 channel is treated in the same way. Neither channel contributes to ordinary local Potts–TIM spin overlaps of R211.
